name: bzip2
one_line: block-sorting file compressor (also bunzip2 and bzcat)
plain: `bzip2` squeezes a file into a smaller .bz2 file. It compresses better than gzip but is slower. `bunzip2` (or `bzip2 -d`) turns it back.
It compresses one file at a time; to pack a folder, use tar with -j, giving .tar.bz2. In CTFs you often meet nested layers (a .bz2 inside a gzip inside a tar), so know all three.
when: Read a compressed file without extracting (bzcat).
Peel layers of a nested archive challenge.

examples.title: Compress a file
examples.explain: Creates notes.txt.bz2 and removes the original unless you use -k.

examples.title: Read without extracting
examples.explain: Prints the uncompressed content to the screen or the pipe.

examples.title: Test a file
examples.explain: -t checks the integrity without writing anything.

examples.title: Compress to standard output
examples.explain: -c writes to the screen (or redirect) and leaves the original alone.

examples.title: Strongest and fastest
examples.explain: -1 to -9 set the block size; 9 is the best and default. --fast is -1.

options.plain: Do not delete the input file.
Try to recover data from a damaged .bz2 file.

mistakes: Expecting bzip2 to archive a folder: it compresses only one file; use tar.
Not using -k and losing the original.
Running bunzip2 on a file that is not really bzip2 (check with file).
Forgetting that format layers can be mixed: run file after every step.
try: Compress a text file with -k and compare sizes with ls -l.
Create a tar.bz2 and list it with tar -tjf.
Make a file compressed three times (gzip, bzip2, gzip) and peel it with file.
